passages.title: A small request within royal control
passages.summary: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon takes Jerusalem and carries off some temple vessels. He orders young men of noble families trained for his court. Daniel and three friends are chosen and given Babylonian names. They are to eat the king’s food and drink his wine. Daniel resolves not to defile himself and asks to be excused. The official fears for his own head. Daniel proposes ten days on vegetables and water. The four look healthier, and God gives them learning and wisdom.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Daniel names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: The 2026 lesson connects faithful choices with resisting harmful pressures. How does the steward’s risk shape Daniel’s proposed trial?

contextNote.title: A small request within royal control
contextNote.text: The four accept new names, a foreign education, and royal service. Verse 8 shows where Daniel draws his line: the king’s table. He decides in his heart, and then he asks. He does not defy the official. His proposal protects that official too (verses 10–13). The test is short, and its result can be checked. The chapter says three times that “God gave” (verses 2, 9, 17).

passages.title: The threatened servants and the fragile statue
passages.summary: The king has a troubling dream and demands that his wise men tell it. They say no one can do this except the gods. He orders all the wise men killed. Daniel asks for time and prays with his friends. God reveals the dream in the night. The king saw a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay. A stone cut without hands struck its feet and became a great mountain. Daniel says God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: The lesson identifies the Church with the kingdom represented by the stone. This is a later Church application of the vision. Why does Daniel pray with his companions before answering?

contextNote.title: The threatened servants and the fragile statue
contextNote.text: The statue’s metals fall in value from the head to the feet. It ends in iron mixed with brittle clay. Verse 34 says the stone was cut “without hands.” No human power made it. Verse 44 says this kingdom will not pass to another people. That sets it apart from every kingdom in the statue. Daniel’s answer saves the other wise men, and he takes no credit (verses 24, 30).

passages.title: Refusal does not depend on rescue
passages.summary: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a huge gold image on a plain. All officials must bow when the music plays, or be thrown into a furnace. Three Jewish officials refuse. The king rages and asks what god can rescue them. They answer that their God is able to save them. Even if he does not, they will not worship the image. They are thrown in, and the king sees four men walking unharmed. He calls them out and praises their God.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: The lesson studies faith that continues even when rescue is uncertain. What makes their refusal independent of rescue?

contextNote.title: Refusal does not depend on rescue
contextNote.text: The king asks in verse 15 what god could rescue them. Their reply has two parts. Verse 17 says their God is able. Verse 18 begins, “But if not.” They do not claim to know what will happen. Their refusal does not depend on being saved. Verse 25 notes that the men walk “loose,” so the fire burned only their ropes.

passages.title: The ruler must learn what his power serves
passages.summary: King Nebuchadnezzar tells this story himself in a letter to all peoples. He dreamed of a great tree that fed and sheltered every creature. A heavenly watcher ordered it cut down, with its stump left in the ground. Daniel explains that the tree is the king. He will live like an animal until he knows that heaven rules. Daniel urges him to do right and show mercy to the poor. A year later the king boasts about Babylon and loses his mind. When he looks up to heaven, his reason returns.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: How does care for poor people relate to royal power?

contextNote.title: The ruler must learn what his power serves
contextNote.text: The tree in the dream gave food and shade to all (verse 12). A king’s greatness was meant to shelter others. Daniel’s advice in verse 27 is specific. The king should do what is right and show mercy to the poor. Verse 29 shows he had twelve months to act. Verse 30 gives his boast: “I have built” and “my power.” The story is told in the voice of the king who learned it.

passages.title: Stolen vessels expose a ruler's blindness
passages.summary: King Belshazzar gives a feast for a thousand nobles. He orders the gold cups from Jerusalem’s temple brought for his guests. They drink and praise gods of gold, silver, wood, and stone. A hand appears and writes on the wall. The king turns pale, and his wise men cannot read it. Daniel is called and refuses the king’s gifts. He reads the words: numbered, weighed, divided. That night Belshazzar is killed.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: Why does Daniel reject the rewards before explaining the writing?

contextNote.title: Stolen vessels expose a ruler's blindness
contextNote.text: Daniel refuses the rewards before he reads a word (verse 17). His message is not for sale. Verse 22 says the king knew what happened to Nebuchadnezzar. Knowing the story did not change him. Verse 23 states the charge in two parts. He used holy cups to praise gods that cannot see or hear. He did not honor the God who holds his breath.

passages.title: Ordinary prayer becomes a legal trap
passages.summary: King Darius appoints officials over the kingdom, and Daniel excels among them. His rivals can find no fault in his work. They persuade the king to ban prayer to anyone but himself for thirty days. Daniel goes home and prays three times a day, as before. The king is distressed and cannot undo his own law. Daniel is thrown to the lions, and the king spends a sleepless night. At dawn Daniel answers that God shut the lions’ mouths. The king orders respect for Daniel’s God.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: The lesson connects Daniel’s regular prayer with daily faith. How does the prayer ban expose the king’s limits?

contextNote.title: Ordinary prayer becomes a legal trap
contextNote.text: Daniel’s rivals build their trap from his known habit (verse 5). Verse 10 says he prayed “as he did before.” He does not hide, and he does not make a display. He simply continues. The law also traps the king who signed it. Verses 14–15 show the most powerful man in the land unable to help. He can only hope that Daniel’s God will (verse 16).

passages.title: The court limits the beasts' power
passages.summary: Daniel dreams of four great beasts rising from a stormy sea. One is like a lion, one like a bear, and one like a leopard. The fourth is terrible, with iron teeth and ten horns. Thrones are set, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat. The court sits, and the books are opened. One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives a lasting kingdom. An angel explains that the beasts are kingdoms. The holy people of the Most High will receive the kingdom.
passages.uncertainty: This vision has no mapped locations. Uncertain settings and unseen conflicts remain unmapped.

lds.text: The lesson reads the humanlike figure through Jesus Christ. This Christian reading remains separate from the vision’s shared kingdom for the saints. Doctrine and Covenants 116 places the Ancient of Days at Adam-ondi-Ahman. Why does the explanation give the kingdom to the saints?

contextNote.title: The court limits the beasts' power
contextNote.text: The kingdoms in this vision appear as animals. The one who finally rules appears as a human figure. Verse 14 says rule “was given” to him; he does not seize it. Verses 9–10 make the turning point a court, not a battle. Verses 18 and 27 give the same kingdom to God’s holy people. Verse 28 says Daniel remained troubled. Jesus draws on this scene in Mark 14:62.

passages.title: Power attacks worship and exhausts the witness
passages.summary: Daniel sees a ram with two horns pushing in every direction. A goat comes from the west and breaks the ram. The goat’s great horn is broken, and four grow in its place. A small horn grows and attacks the holy place and its daily offering. A voice asks how long this will last. Gabriel explains that the ram is Media and Persia and the goat is Greece. A fierce king will rise and be broken without human hand. Daniel is sick for days and does not understand.
passages.uncertainty: This vision has no mapped locations. Uncertain settings and unseen conflicts remain unmapped.

lds.text: What remains difficult after the animals receive named explanations?

contextNote.title: Power attacks worship and exhausts the witness
contextNote.text: Gabriel comes close, and Daniel falls on his face in fear (verse 17). The angel then names the kingdoms outright (verses 20–21). That is rare in visions of this kind. Even so, verse 27 says Daniel was ill and did not understand. Named explanations do not remove the weight of what he saw. Verse 25 says the last king is broken “without hand.” The stone of 2:34 was described the same way.

passages.title: Confession asks for mercy beyond earned reward
passages.summary: Daniel reads in Jeremiah that Jerusalem’s ruin would last seventy years. He turns to God with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes. He confesses that all Israel has sinned and ignored the prophets. God is in the right, and shame belongs to the people. He asks God to turn his anger from Jerusalem. He asks on the ground of mercy and for God’s own name. Gabriel comes while he is still praying. He speaks of seventy weeks set for the people and the holy city.
passages.uncertainty: City markers locate named references. They do not trace the movements of visions.

lds.text: Why does Daniel appeal to mercy rather than earned reward?

contextNote.title: Confession asks for mercy beyond earned reward
contextNote.text: Verse 2 shows the prayer beginning from a text, the scroll of Jeremiah. The story has shown Daniel as faithful, yet he says “we” throughout. Verse 18 states his ground plainly. He does not ask because the people deserve it. He asks because God’s mercies are great. Verse 19 adds that the city and people carry God’s name. Readers have understood the seventy weeks of verses 24–27 in very different ways.

passages.title: The unseen conflict meets a weakened body
passages.summary: In the third year of Cyrus, Daniel mourns for three weeks. Beside the Tigris he sees a man clothed in linen with a face like lightning. His companions run, and Daniel falls weak to the ground. A hand lifts him to his knees. The messenger says Daniel’s words were heard from the first day. The prince of Persia opposed him for twenty-one days until Michael came. Daniel cannot speak or breathe. The messenger touches him again and says, “Peace be to you.”
passages.uncertainty: This vision has no mapped locations. Uncertain settings and unseen conflicts remain unmapped.

lds.text: How does the messenger help Daniel’s weakened body?

contextNote.title: The unseen conflict meets a weakened body
contextNote.text: Daniel mourned and fasted for three full weeks (verses 2–3). Verse 12 says his words were heard on the first day. Verse 13 explains the delay as a conflict he could not see. It lasted twenty-one days, the same three weeks. The wait is not blamed on the one who prayed. The messenger touches him three times (verses 10, 16, 18). Each touch restores a little more of his strength.

passages.title: Broken alliances do not stop faithful teaching
passages.summary: The messenger describes a long line of kings. A mighty king rises, and his kingdom is divided to the four winds. Kings of the south and north make war and marriage alliances that fail. A hateful ruler gains power by flattery. He attacks the holy covenant and stops the daily offering. Those who know their God stand firm and act. The wise teach many, though some fall by sword and flame. The proud king exalts himself and comes to his end with no one to help.
passages.uncertainty: This vision has no mapped locations. Uncertain settings and unseen conflicts remain unmapped.

lds.text: Why does faithful teaching remain important when teachers suffer?

contextNote.title: Broken alliances do not stop faithful teaching
contextNote.text: Verses 32–33 describe faithful people under a violent ruler. They know their God, stand firm, and teach others. Verse 33 admits that they fall by sword, fire, and prison. Verse 35 gives that suffering a purpose and a limit. It refines them, and it lasts only until the appointed time. Their fall is not counted as failure. The alliances earlier in the chapter all collapse (verses 6 and 17).

passages.title: Hope includes waiting without full understanding
passages.summary: The messenger says a time of great trouble is coming. Daniel’s people will be rescued, all whose names are written in the book. Many who sleep in the dust will awake. Some rise to lasting life, and some to shame. The wise will shine like the sky. Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end. He hears and does not understand, and he asks about the outcome. He is told to go his way, rest, and rise at the end.
passages.uncertainty: This vision has no mapped locations. Uncertain settings and unseen conflicts remain unmapped.

lds.text: What does Daniel receive when full understanding remains unavailable?

contextNote.title: Hope includes waiting without full understanding
contextNote.text: Verse 2 gives the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament. Verse 3 names those who will shine. They are the wise who turn many to righteousness. These are the teachers of 11:33, some of whom were killed. In verse 8 Daniel says he does not understand and asks more. Verse 9 does not explain. Verse 13 gives him a promise for himself: rest, and a place at the end.

events.title: The unseen conflict meets a weakened body
events.summary: In the third year of Cyrus, Daniel mourns for three weeks. Beside the Tigris he sees a man clothed in linen with a face like lightning. His companions run, and Daniel falls weak to the ground. A hand lifts him to his knees. The messenger says Daniel’s words were heard from the first day. The prince of Persia opposed him for twenty-one days until Michael came. Daniel cannot speak or breathe. The messenger touches him again and says, “Peace be to you.”
events.detail: Daniel mourned and fasted for three full weeks (verses 2–3). Verse 12 says his words were heard on the first day. Verse 13 explains the delay as a conflict he could not see. It lasted twenty-one days, the same three weeks. The wait is not blamed on the one who prayed. The messenger touches him three times (verses 10, 16, 18). Each touch restores a little more of his strength.

lds.text: How does the messenger help Daniel’s weakened body?

events.title: Broken alliances do not stop faithful teaching
events.summary: The messenger describes a long line of kings. A mighty king rises, and his kingdom is divided to the four winds. Kings of the south and north make war and marriage alliances that fail. A hateful ruler gains power by flattery. He attacks the holy covenant and stops the daily offering. Those who know their God stand firm and act. The wise teach many, though some fall by sword and flame. The proud king exalts himself and comes to his end with no one to help.
events.detail: Verses 32–33 describe faithful people under a violent ruler. They know their God, stand firm, and teach others. Verse 33 admits that they fall by sword, fire, and prison. Verse 35 gives that suffering a purpose and a limit. It refines them, and it lasts only until the appointed time. Their fall is not counted as failure. The alliances earlier in the chapter all collapse (verses 6 and 17).

events.title: Hope includes waiting without full understanding
events.summary: The messenger says a time of great trouble is coming. Daniel’s people will be rescued, all whose names are written in the book. Many who sleep in the dust will awake. Some rise to lasting life, and some to shame. The wise will shine like the sky. Daniel is told to seal the book until the time of the end. He hears and does not understand, and he asks about the outcome. He is told to go his way, rest, and rise at the end.
events.detail: Verse 2 gives the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament. Verse 3 names those who will shine. They are the wise who turn many to righteousness. These are the teachers of 11:33, some of whom were killed. In verse 8 Daniel says he does not understand and asks more. Verse 9 does not explain. Verse 13 gives him a promise for himself: rest, and a place at the end.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

guides.title: Daniel: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Refusal does not depend on rescue
steps.text: The king asks in verse 15 what god could rescue them. Their reply has two parts. Verse 17 says their God is able. Verse 18 begins, “But if not.” They do not claim to know what will happen. Their refusal does not depend on being saved. Verse 25 notes that the men walk “loose,” so the fire burned only their ropes.

steps.title: The court limits the beasts' power
steps.text: The kingdoms in this vision appear as animals. The one who finally rules appears as a human figure. Verse 14 says rule “was given” to him; he does not seize it. Verses 9–10 make the turning point a court, not a battle. Verses 18 and 27 give the same kingdom to God’s holy people. Verse 28 says Daniel remained troubled. Jesus draws on this scene in Mark 14:62.

steps.title: Hope includes waiting without full understanding
steps.text: Verse 2 gives the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament. Verse 3 names those who will shine. They are the wise who turn many to righteousness. These are the teachers of 11:33, some of whom were killed. In verse 8 Daniel says he does not understand and asks more. Verse 9 does not explain. Verse 13 gives him a promise for himself: rest, and a place at the end.

chapterMaps.note: Lines join the places Daniel names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.
chapterMaps.narrative: Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon takes Jerusalem and carries off some temple vessels. He orders young men of noble families trained for his court. Daniel and three friends are chosen and given Babylonian names. They are to eat the king’s food and drink his wine. Daniel resolves not to defile himself and asks to be excused. The official fears for his own head. Daniel proposes ten days on vegetables and water. The four look healthier, and God gives them learning and wisdom.

chapterMaps.narrative: The king has a troubling dream and demands that his wise men tell it. They say no one can do this except the gods. He orders all the wise men killed. Daniel asks for time and prays with his friends. God reveals the dream in the night. The king saw a statue of gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay. A stone cut without hands struck its feet and became a great mountain. Daniel says God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed.

chapterMaps.narrative: Nebuchadnezzar sets up a huge gold image on a plain. All officials must bow when the music plays, or be thrown into a furnace. Three Jewish officials refuse. The king rages and asks what god can rescue them. They answer that their God is able to save them. Even if he does not, they will not worship the image. They are thrown in, and the king sees four men walking unharmed. He calls them out and praises their God.

chapterMaps.narrative: King Nebuchadnezzar tells this story himself in a letter to all peoples. He dreamed of a great tree that fed and sheltered every creature. A heavenly watcher ordered it cut down, with its stump left in the ground. Daniel explains that the tree is the king. He will live like an animal until he knows that heaven rules. Daniel urges him to do right and show mercy to the poor. A year later the king boasts about Babylon and loses his mind. When he looks up to heaven, his reason returns.

chapterMaps.narrative: King Belshazzar gives a feast for a thousand nobles. He orders the gold cups from Jerusalem’s temple brought for his guests. They drink and praise gods of gold, silver, wood, and stone. A hand appears and writes on the wall. The king turns pale, and his wise men cannot read it. Daniel is called and refuses the king’s gifts. He reads the words: numbered, weighed, divided. That night Belshazzar is killed.

chapterMaps.narrative: King Darius appoints officials over the kingdom, and Daniel excels among them. His rivals can find no fault in his work. They persuade the king to ban prayer to anyone but himself for thirty days. Daniel goes home and prays three times a day, as before. The king is distressed and cannot undo his own law. Daniel is thrown to the lions, and the king spends a sleepless night. At dawn Daniel answers that God shut the lions’ mouths. The king orders respect for Daniel’s God.

chapterMaps.narrative: Daniel dreams of four great beasts rising from a stormy sea. One is like a lion, one like a bear, and one like a leopard. The fourth is terrible, with iron teeth and ten horns. Thrones are set, and the Ancient of Days takes his seat. The court sits, and the books are opened. One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives a lasting kingdom. An angel explains that the beasts are kingdoms. The holy people of the Most High will receive the kingdom.

A small horn grows and attacks the holy place and its daily offering. A voice asks how long this will last. Gabriel explains that the ram is Media and Persia and the goat is Greece. A fierce king will rise and be broken without human hand. Daniel is sick for days and does not understand.

chapterMaps.narrative: Daniel reads in Jeremiah that Jerusalem’s ruin would last seventy years. He turns to God with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes. He confesses that all Israel has sinned and ignored the prophets. God is in the right, and shame belongs to the people. He asks God to turn his anger from Jerusalem. He asks on the ground of mercy and for God’s own name. Gabriel comes while he is still praying. He speaks of seventy weeks set for the people and the holy city.
